You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test case `testInfiniteLoop()` triggers a call to `HelpFormatter.printHelp` with the width set to 20 and an option with a long description that doesn't fit within this width. This corresponds exactly to the issue described in the current bug report, where HelpFormatter goes into an infinite loop when a single word is longer than the allowed width.

Looking at the relevant code in `HelpFormatter`:
- `printHelp` calls `printOptions`.
- `printOptions` builds up a string of the options and their descriptions by calling `renderOptions`.
- `renderOptions` builds option lines with descriptions concatenated and then calls `renderWrappedText` to wrap the text to the specified width.
- `renderWrappedText` attempts to split the given text into lines according to the width by using `findWrapPos`.
- The code attempts to handle wrapping by repeatedly finding a wrap position and appending wrapped lines until no wrap is needed.
- However, if the position to wrap (`pos`) remains the same on consecutive iterations (indicating no progress in wrapping the text), the code detects the infinite loop condition and throws an explicit RuntimeException with a message about avoiding infinite loop (CLI-162).

The original behavior according to the bug report is that `HelpFormatter` hangs or crashes with `OutOfMemoryError` due to infinite looping when a word is too long for the line. This seems caused by `renderWrappedText` not correctly handling the condition where a single, very long word cannot be wrapped because there's no suitable break point within the given width. 

The fix that appears in the code snippet of `renderWrappedText` is the addition of the check:
```java
if (pos == lastPos)
{
    throw new RuntimeException("Text too long for line - throwing exception to avoid infinite loop [CLI-162]: " + text);
}
```
This condition explicitly throws instead of allowing an infinite loop, indicating a fix attempt for the reported bug CLI-162.

In summary:
- Wrapping code in `HelpFormatter.renderWrappedText` tries to wrap text to width.
- When text contains a single unwrappable word longer than width, it previously would loop infinitely.
- Now the code detects this case and throws an exception to avoid infinite looping.
- The test case demonstrates the problematic scenario for long word description running with small width value.
- The bug report explicitly states that the old implementation hangs or crashes due to infinite looping in this wrapping code.
- The provided snippet shows the current state with a guard to prevent infinite loop by throwing an exception.

Therefore, the root cause of the failure is that prior to this emergency guard, `renderWrappedText` did not properly handle words longer than the specified width, causing an infinite loop in wrapping logic triggered by the test case input. The guard resolves hanging by throwing an explicit exception instead.

The places directly involved and relevant for correctness and fix are:
- `HelpFormatter.renderWrappedText` where the infinite loop occurs
- The higher-level method `HelpFormatter.renderOptions` which calls the wrapping code for option descriptions
- Possibly `printHelp` as the entry point to printing help messages with options

Recent bug reports do not appear relevant to this particular wrapping infinite loop issue.

# Final diagnosis
The infinite loop happens in `HelpFormatter.renderWrappedText` because if the method tries to wrap a single word that exceeds the maximum line width, the calculation of wrapping position never advances and causes a loop. Previously there was no detection of this condition, causing JVM crash due to exhaustion. The current code shows the fix adding explicit detection and throwing an exception to prevent endless looping in such scenarios.

This clarifies that the root cause is a missing or inadequate guard in the wrapping algorithm when handling words longer than the allowed wrap width. The fix must be in or around `HelpFormatter.renderWrappedText` to correctly break or handle such words and avoid infinite loops.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
